interviewQuestions.question: What is memory coalescing and why does it matter for GPU performance?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
⭐ **Q: What is memory coalescing and why does it matter for GPU performance?**

I'd start with the mechanism: when threads within a warp access memory, the hardware checks whether their addresses are adjacent. If thread 0 reads element 0, thread 1 reads element 1, and so on, the memory controller merges all those requests into a single wide transaction. If the addresses are scattered or strided instead, that same warp generates up to 32 separate transactions.

Why it matters: the difference between coalesced and uncoalesced access can be an order of magnitude in effective bandwidth, even though the compute logic and parallelism are identical in both cases. A very common real example is iterating a matrix in the wrong dimension relative to its storage layout — row-major data accessed column-wise breaks coalescing even though the algorithm is otherwise correct.

I'd close with the practical implication: when a GPU kernel underperforms its theoretical peak, checking the memory access pattern is usually the first thing I'd look at, before touching the compute logic at all.

**Testing:** whether you understand that GPU bandwidth is conditional on access pattern, not just data volume — a frequent gap for people who've only worked with CPU-side performance tuning.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Coalescing and effective bandwidth

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through the GPU memory hierarchy and when you'd use shared memory versus relying on global memory directly.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
**Q: Walk me through the GPU memory hierarchy and when you'd use shared memory versus relying on global memory directly.**

I'd lay it out from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest: registers (per-thread, fastest), shared memory (per-block, on-chip scratchpad, programmer-managed), and global memory (grid-wide, large, but hundreds of cycles of latency).

I'd reach for shared memory whenever multiple threads *in the same block* need the same piece of global data — the classic case is a tiled matrix multiply, where each tile is loaded into shared memory once and then reused by every thread in the block, instead of each thread independently re-fetching the same values from slow global memory. If data isn't reused across threads in a block, shared memory just adds complexity with no payoff — plain (coalesced) global memory access is fine.

I'd also flag register spilling as a trap: if a kernel uses too many per-thread variables, the compiler spills the overflow into local memory, which physically lives in global DRAM — so a kernel can look like it's using fast registers while actually generating slow memory traffic.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about when the added complexity of shared memory actually pays off, not just recite the hierarchy from memory.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Choosing shared vs global memory
